property_summary: For every caller/address input, the reference contract's owner() returns the actual stored owner (non-zero after construction), whereas the mutant returns address(0), so owner() should never be zero for the reference but is zero for the mutant for some inputs.

For any deployer address used when constructing C, the reference contract's owner() returns the deployer (non-zero) while the mutant returns address(0), so owner() must equal the deployer address for all inputs — the bug makes owner() sometimes zero and thus not equal to the deployer.

For every deployment of C with any liquidityReceiveAddress, owner() must be a non-zero address (the contract sets an owner in constructor); the mutant returns zero address instead, violating this rule for some inputs.
For any deployment, C.owner() (the public getter) always returns a non-zero address in the reference implementation; the mutant returns address(0) breaking this rule for some inputs.

For any fuzzed address input X passed to C.owner() (i.e. any caller), the reference contract always returns a non-zero owner address (the stored owner), whereas the mutant sometimes returns address(0); the test asserts owner() != address(0) for every call (which holds for the reference) so the mutant fails for some inputs.

Reference contract rejects transferring ownership to the zero address (transferOwnership(address(0)) reverts), whereas the mutant allows transferring ownership to address(0); therefore for all callers the reference's transferOwnership(address(0)) call must fail, but the mutant will succeed for some inputs.

For any caller that is the current owner, calling transferOwnership(newOwner) must revert if newOwner == address(0) (reference enforces non-zero new owner), but the mutant allows transferOwnership(address(0)) to succeed, so the property is that transferOwnership(address(0)) always reverts for owner callers in the reference and the mutant breaks this.

For every caller equal to the current owner, calling transferOwnership with any fuzzed address that is equal to the contract's own address MUST succeed on the reference but the mutant (which allows zero) will differ when the fuzzed address is zero — we instead assert a universal property: for any fuzzed newOwner, calling transferOwnership(newOwner) from the current owner either reverts iff newOwner == address(0) in the reference; equivalently, the reference never sets owner to address(0) so after a transferOwnership(newOwner) call the owner is never address(0) — the mutant can set owner to address(0) for some input.

For the correct contract, after any transferOwnership(newOwner) call made by the current owner, owner() is never address(0); the mutant (which removed the non-zero check) allows owner() == address(0) for some fuzzed newOwner, so the property is violated.

For every non-owner caller, transferOwnership(newOwner) must revert; the mutant still allows the current owner to set owner to address(0) — instead we assert a universal property: when called by a non-owner, transferOwnership(newOwner) always reverts (reference) but the mutant can violate ownership-based access control for some fuzzed owner by changing who is owner via prior calls, so the fuzzer finds a sequence where a non-owner call succeeds on mutant but reference still reverts; we encode this by fuzzing an address that we attempt to make owner via a prior owner call and then assert a non-owner cannot call transferOwnership afterwards.

For any caller, calling transferOwnership(newOwner) on the correct contract succeeds iff the caller is the contract owner (onlyOwner), and additionally the correct contract allows the owner to set any non-zero newOwner; the mutant wrongly rejects non-owner callers only when they try to set non-zero newOwner (adds extra require), so there exist inputs (caller != owner and newOwner == address(0)) where behavior differs — specifically the mutant disallows setting a non-zero owner by non-owner callers leading to different success/failure outcomes when transferOwnership is attempted with various callers and newOwner addresses.

For any caller address and target newOwner, the reference contract allows transferOwnership to succeed exactly when the caller is the current owner and newOwner is non-zero; the mutant additionally requires that if the caller is not the owner then newOwner must be zero, causing calls by non-owners with non-zero newOwner to revert while the reference would not be callable (but both enforce onlyOwner) — therefore the observable difference is whether transferOwnership called by the owner with a non-zero newOwner succeeds (reference: succeeds) versus the mutant (will also succeed) — to expose the mutant we fuzz caller and newOwner and check that onlyOwner restriction still applies and that when called via try/catch the outcome for owner vs non-owner/newOwner zero vs non-zero differs, revealing the mutant rejects certain inputs the reference would accept via try/catch observation.

For every caller and candidate newOwner, calling transferOwnership(newOwner) only succeeds when the caller is the current owner and newOwner != address(0); the reference always enforces onlyOwner and non-zero newOwner (so owner can set any non-zero new owner), whereas the mutant adds an extra check that forbids non-owner callers from proposing a non-zero newOwner which makes the observable success/failure pattern (when fuzzing caller and newOwner) differ for some inputs.

For all callers and candidate newOwner addresses, transferOwnership(newOwner) succeeds iff the caller is the current owner and newOwner != address(0); the mutant introduces an extra restriction that non-owners may only pass newOwner==address(0), causing a different success/failure pattern for some (caller, newOwner) fuzzed inputs.

For any caller and newOwner, transferOwnership(newOwner) succeeds exactly when the caller is the current owner and newOwner != address(0); the mutant adds a restriction that non-owners may only supply newOwner == address(0), causing a different success/failure pattern for some fuzzed (caller,newOwner) inputs.

For any caller address X, in the correct contract transferOwnership(X) only succeeds when called by the current owner (onlyOwner requires caller == owner), but the mutant inverts that check so some non-owner callers (or the owner) can succeed differently; therefore for all callers the reference will only allow the owner to transfer ownership while the mutant allows at least one non-owner to succeed — test checks whether calling transferOwnership from a non-owner can succeed.

For any caller address X, only the current owner may successfully call transferOwnership in the reference contract; the mutant inverts the check and therefore allows at least one non-owner caller to successfully transfer ownership for some inputs.

Reference: only the current owner can successfully call transferOwnership; Buggy mutant (inverted onlyOwner) allows a non-owner caller to successfully invoke transferOwnership for some caller address, so there exists a caller for which transferOwnership succeeds on the mutant but not on the reference.

Invariant: only the current owner can successfully call transferOwnership on the reference contract for every caller; the mutant inverts the onlyOwner check allowing at least one non-owner caller to successfully call transferOwnership for some input (so a non-owner can change owner on the mutant but not on the reference).

Invariant: transferOwnership can only be successfully executed when the caller is the current owner in the reference contract for every caller; the mutant inverts the onlyOwner check and therefore allows at least one non-owner caller to successfully call transferOwnership (changing owner) — the test fuzzes a caller and asserts that a non-owner call cannot succeed.

For every call, the reference contract's name() returns the ERC20 token name stored at construction (not a hardcoded different string); the mutant returns a different hardcoded string for some inputs, so the returned string must differ.

For every input address x, calling c.name() returns the token's stored name string (the name set in constructor) in the reference; the mutant returns a different hardcoded string for some inputs, so there exists an input where the two return values differ.

For every input string s passed to the contract's name() via Solidity ABI decoding (i.e. any calldata shape that results in a successful external call to name()), the reference contract returns the stored token name string set at construction, whereas the mutant returns the hardcoded different string for some calldata—so the returned string must equal the stored name for all successful calls in the reference but not in the mutant.

For every calldata bytes input that successfully calls C.name() (i.e. any calldata whose selector matches the public name() function), the reference contract returns the stored token name string set at construction; the mutant returns a different hardcoded string for some such calldata, so there exist calldata bytes where returned strings differ.

For every input calldata that successfully invokes C.name(), the reference returns the token name stored at construction ("DCF Token"); the mutant sometimes returns a different literal ("MUTATED_NAME"), so there exist inputs where the returned string differs.

For any caller address, C.symbol() returns the token's stored symbol string (_symbol) (so calling symbol() always returns the deployed token's symbol); the mutant returns a hardcoded different string for some inputs (callers), breaking this equality.
